If You Only Remember These

Pages 1–8
  1. β blockers competitively block β receptors → inhibit adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP.
  2. Nonselective first generation: propranolol, nadolol, timolol, pindolol, penbutolol.
  3. β1-selective second generation: metoprolol, atenolol, esmolol, acebutolol, bisoprolol. Selectivity falls at high doses.
  4. Third generation with extra actions: carvedilol, labetalol, bucindolol, carteolol are nonselective. Nebivolol, betaxolol, celiprolol are β1-selective.
  5. ISA = partial agonist action. Prototype is pindolol. ISA drugs are less likely to cause bradycardia.
  6. MSA = local anesthetic or quinidine-like action from Na+ channel blockade. It is undesirable for topical ocular use because it can blunt protective corneal reflexes.
  7. Short-acting standout: esmolol, IV, half-life about 10–15 minutes, rapidly hydrolyzed by RBC esterases.
  8. Long-acting standouts: nadolol and nebivolol.
  9. Acute nonselective β2 blockade can raise PVR because α1 vasoconstriction becomes unopposed.
  10. Long-term antihypertensive effects include sustained ↓ PVR, ↓ renin release, and in some drugs peripheral vasodilation.
  11. Pheochromocytoma: establish adequate α blockade before β blockade to avoid unopposed α agonism and hypertensive crisis.
  12. Major adverse effect in asthma: bronchoconstriction from β2 blockade. The lecture advises avoiding β blockers in asthma when possible.
  13. Nonselective β blockers can prolong hypoglycemia and mask warning signs. β1-selective agents are preferred when a β blocker is required in diabetes.
  14. Never abruptly stop chronic β blockers. Upregulated β receptors can produce rebound tachycardia, hypertension, worsening angina, and occasionally MI.
  15. Open-angle glaucoma: topical β blockers ↓ aqueous humor production → ↓ cAMP → ↓ IOP. Timolol is the classic nonselective agent.
  16. Propranolol: highly lipophilic, extensive first-pass metabolism, low oral bioavailability, performance anxiety, thyroid storm, migraine prophylaxis.
  17. Metoprolol: β1-selective prototype. Nebivolol: most highly β1-selective in the lecture, plus β3 agonism and NO-mediated vasodilation.
  18. Labetalol and carvedilol: mixed α1 plus β blockade. Labetalol is used for hypertensive emergencies and chronic hypertension in pregnancy.

MUST KNOW ISA, MSA, lipid solubility, vasodilation

Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, ISA
  • Partial β agonist action
  • Blocks strong catecholamine stimulation but moderately activates β receptors when endogenous agonist is absent
  • Prototype: Pindolol
  • Also: Acebutolol, Labetalol, Carteolol, Oxprenolol, Penbutolol, Celiprolol
Membrane stabilizing activity, MSA
  • Local anesthetic or quinidine-like action
  • Mechanism: Na+ channel blockade
  • Examples: Propranolol, Carvedilol, Acebutolol, Labetalol, Metoprolol, Pindolol
  • Undesirable for topical eye use
Lipid solubility
  • High: Propranolol, Penbutolol
  • Moderate: Metoprolol, Carvedilol, Timolol, Pindolol
  • Low: Nebivolol, Nadolol, Atenolol, Esmolol, Labetalol, Betaxolol, Acebutolol, Bisoprolol
Vasodilating β blockers
  • Carvedilol, Labetalol, Nebivolol, Celiprolol, and several others listed in the lecture
  • The lecture specifically says carvedilol vasodilation is linked to nitric oxide production, not simply its α blockade
  • Mixed α1 + β blockers: Carvedilol, Labetalol, Bucindolol
Do not confuse: β1-selective does not mean β1-only.
The lecture repeatedly emphasizes that receptor selectivity is dose related. At higher concentrations, β1-selective blockers can also block β2 receptors.

SHOULD KNOW The 7 distinguishing properties used by the lecture

  1. Relative affinity for β1 and β2 receptors
  2. Intrinsic sympathetic activity, meaning partial agonistic action
  3. Degree of lipid solubility
  4. Membrane stabilizing activity, meaning local anesthetic or quinidine-like action
  5. Vasodilating action
  6. Mixed adrenoceptor blockade involving α1 plus β1 and β2
  7. Other PK differences, including oral bioavailability, half-life, duration of action, and protein binding

2. Pharmacokinetics
Mark complete
Page 2, Appendix page 9

MUST KNOW Absorption and bioavailability

  • Most β blockers are well absorbed orally and peak in about 1–3 hours.
  • Propranolol has low oral bioavailability because of extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism.
  • Propranolol hepatic extraction can become saturated, so plasma level and oral bioavailability rise as the dose increases.
  • Sustained-release preparations exist for propranolol and metoprolol, allowing once-daily dosing.
  • Lecture-listed bioavailability exceptions: Betaxolol, Pindolol, Penbutolol, Sotalol.

MUST KNOW Distribution and clearance

Lipophilic
  • Large volume of distribution due to tissue uptake
  • Can cross the BBB and cause CNS effects
  • Highly lipophilic: Propranolol, Penbutolol
  • Moderately lipophilic: Metoprolol, Carvedilol
Hydrophilic
  • Lower volume of distribution
  • Do not readily cross the BBB in the lecture framing
  • Nadolol, Atenolol, Esmolol
Esmolol
IV infusion → rapid hydrolysis by red blood cell esterases → half-life about 10–15 min → rapid onset and rapid termination after stopping infusion

SHOULD KNOW Metabolism

  • CYP2D6 genotype is a major determinant of interindividual differences in plasma clearance.
  • Extensively metabolized in liver: Propranolol, Metoprolol.
  • Less completely metabolized: Celiprolol, Atenolol, Pindolol.
  • Not appreciably metabolized: Nadolol, Carteolol, excreted unchanged in urine.
  • Poor CYP2D6 metabolizers can have markedly higher metoprolol plasma concentrations.
Fast PK cue: Esmolol = shortest. Nadolol and nebivolol = long acting. Propranolol = lipophilic + first-pass. Nadolol = hydrophilic + renal elimination.

NICE TO KNOW Structural and elimination details not to lose

  • Most β blockers are described as structurally similar to catecholamines and to isoproterenol, but with opposing action.
  • The lecture emphasizes bulky alkyl substitution on nitrogen and the oxymethylene bridge near the aromatic ring.
  • L-isomers are identified as the active forms.
  • Elimination can be prolonged by liver disease, decreased hepatic blood flow, hepatic enzyme inhibitors, or renal dysfunction.
  • Nadolol is specifically described elsewhere in the lecture as requiring dose reduction in renal failure because of drug accumulation.

Recall Check

Which β blocker has the shortest half-life?

Esmolol, about 10–15 minutes.

Which CYP genotype is emphasized as a major source of interindividual clearance differences?

CYP2D6.

Why is oral propranolol dose substantially higher than IV dose?

Extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability.

3. Pharmacodynamics and Cardiovascular Effects
Mark complete
Pages 2–3

MUST KNOW Core mechanism

β blocker binds β receptor competitively → ↓ adenylyl cyclase activity → ↓ cAMP → reduced β-receptor-mediated cellular response

The lecture also notes inverse agonism for betaxolol, metoprolol, propranolol, and nadolol, meaning they reduce constitutive β-receptor activity by stabilizing the inactive receptor state.

MUST KNOW Cardiovascular effects

  • β1 blockade → ↓ myocardial force of contraction + ↓ HR.
  • Usually little BP effect in normotensive people, but BP falls in hypertension.
  • During exercise or stress, β1 blockade blunts the expected rise in HR.
  • Short term: ↓ cardiac output. With nonselective agents, β2 blockade can increase PVR through unopposed α1 vasoconstriction.
  • Long term: TPR may normalize or remain reduced, contributing to antihypertensive action.

Antihypertensive mechanisms

1. Sustained ↓ PVR
Long-term vascular adaptation contributes substantially to ↓ BP.
2. ↓ Renin
β1 blockade in JG cells → ↓ renin → ↓ RAAS stimulation → ↓ BP.
3. Central sympathetic outflow
Proposed, but the lecture says evidence is limited.
4. ↓ NE release
Blocking presynaptic facilitatory β receptors may reduce norepinephrine release.
5. Peripheral vasodilation
Some agents increase NO-mediated vasodilation, including nebivolol, celiprolol, carvedilol.
Exam trap: Pindolol and renin. The lecture states that pindolol has little or no effect on plasma renin activity.

MUST KNOW Nonselective β blockers and pressor responses

Recall BP = CO × PVR. α1 stimulation raises PVR through vasoconstriction. β2 stimulation lowers PVR through vasodilation.

Nonselective β blockade → β2 vasodilation blocked → α1 vasoconstriction becomes relatively unopposed → augmented pressor response to epinephrine
Pheochromocytoma: β blocker only after adequate α blockade. Otherwise catecholamines can strongly stimulate unblocked α receptors, producing severe vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis.

Recall Check

What happens to renin with β1 blockade?

Renin decreases, which reduces RAAS stimulation.

Why can a nonselective β blocker increase PVR acutely?

β2-mediated vasodilation is blocked, leaving unopposed α1 vasoconstriction.

What must precede β blockade in pheochromocytoma?

Adequate α receptor blockade.

4. Cardioselectivity, ISA, MSA, Metabolic Effects, Toxicity
Mark complete
Pages 3–4

MUST KNOW Cardioselective β1 blockers

Preferred by the lecture when a β blocker is required in patients with bronchospasm, diabetes, or peripheral vascular disease or Raynaud phenomenon.

Mnemonic from the lecture: NAME CAB = Nebivolol, Atenolol, Metoprolol, Esmolol, Celiprolol, Acebutolol, Betaxolol.

Metoprolol is equipotent to propranolol at β1 blockade but about 50–100 fold less potent at β2 blockade.

MUST KNOW ISA advantages and downside

Potential advantage in lectureImportant downside
Less bradycardiaMay precipitate angina by increasing oxygen demand through tachycardia and increased myocardial workload.
May be useful in diminished cardiac reserve
May be useful in patients prone to symptomatic bradycardia
Less β2 blockade burden in asthma and peripheral vasospastic disease
Lecture also lists diabetes as a setting where partial agonism may be useful

ISA mnemonic from the lecture: APO CAP = Alprenolol, Pindolol, Oxprenolol, Carteolol, Acebutolol, Penbutolol.

MUST KNOW Respiratory and glucose effects

Bronchospasm
  • Major adverse effect in asthma from β2 blockade
  • Can be life-threatening in asthma or COPD
  • β1-selective blockers are less likely to induce bronchospasm, but the lecture still recommends avoiding β blockers in asthma when possible
Hypoglycemia
  • β2 blockade partially inhibits hepatic glycogenolysis
  • Nonselective blockers can delay recovery from insulin-induced hypoglycemia
  • They may mask warning signs such as tremor, tachycardia, sweating, nervousness
  • β1-selective agents are preferred if a β blocker is necessary

SHOULD KNOW Lipid effects

β1 and β3 blockade → ↓ adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP → ↓ triglyceride lipase activity → ↓ FFA release

Nonselective β blockers: ↓ HDL, ↑ VLDL, ↑ triglycerides, with LDL generally unchanged. Newer blockers listed as less likely to have negative metabolic effects are carvedilol, nebivolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol.

MUST KNOW Adverse effects

SystemKey adverse effectsHigh-yield note
CardiovascularBradycardia, cold extremities, hypotension, heart failure, cardiac decompensationBradycardia is the most common adverse cardiac effect. Lecture treatment: atropine, often pacemaker if needed.
CNSMild sedation, vivid dreams, nightmares, fatigue, rare depressionLess likely with hydrophilic low-lipid-solubility drugs such as nadolol, atenolol, esmolol.
RespiratoryWorsening asthma and obstructive airway diseaseMostly a problem with nonselective blockade.
Endocrine and metabolicHypoglycemia, slight weight gain, negative lipid changes, sexual dysfunctionHypoglycemia risk is greater with nonselective agents.
Withdrawal syndrome: abrupt discontinuation after long-term use → β-receptor upregulation and supersensitivity → nervousness, tachycardia, ↑ BP, worsening angina, possible MI. The lecture advises gradual dose reduction over several weeks and restricted exercise during tapering.

SHOULD KNOW Membrane-stabilizing effects on cardiac conduction

  • ↓ sinus rate and ↓ spontaneous depolarization of ectopic pacemakers
  • Slower AV nodal and atrial conduction
  • ↑ functional refractory period of the AV node and prolongation of the PR interval
  • Generalized suppression of myocardial function

SHOULD KNOW Lecture table placed under MSA

Lecture-listed potential advantagesLecture-listed disadvantages
  • Early use after acute MI for prevention of recurrent MI and sudden death
  • Lecture states about 25% mortality reduction with chronic use in post-MI and HFrEF patients
  • Examples listed in that row: Metoprolol, Atenolol, Timolol
  • Limits infarct size and may improve survival
  • ↓ myocardial O2 demand, redistribution of myocardial blood flow, antiarrhythmic actions
  • Examples listed: Propranolol, Alprenolol, Labetalol, Oxprenolol, Carvedilol, Acebutolol
  • May convert latent CHF to overt CHF
  • Not desirable for topical ocular use because corneal local anesthesia may remove protective reflexes

Audit note: the lecture places this table under MSA even though some named drugs elsewhere are listed as having little or no MSA. This reviewer does not resolve that inconsistency.

NICE TO KNOW Supplementary material explicitly marked as outside Dr. Reyes' PowerPoint

The lecture notes say this subsection came from Katzung and a 2022A trans rather than the PowerPoint.

  • Partial β agonist activity was described as helping avoid excessive bradycardia or asthma precipitation, but as not equivalent to pure antagonists for secondary MI prevention.
  • Named ISA drugs here: Acebutolol, Carteolol, Celiprolol, Labetalol, Penbutolol, Pindolol.
  • Local anesthetic action was described for Acebutolol, Pindolol, Propranolol, Labetalol, Metoprolol, with slight effect for Betaxolol.
  • The same ocular warning is repeated: local anesthetic action can eliminate the protective corneal reflex.

SHOULD KNOW Drug-specific details from pages 4–6

Propranolol
  • Almost completely absorbed orally but with low systemic availability because of first-pass metabolism
  • Hepatic extraction is saturable, so bioavailability rises with dose
  • Food and long-term administration are stated to increase oral bioavailability
  • Active metabolite: 4-hydroxypropranolol with weak β-antagonist activity
  • Lecture also lists uterine contraction, prolonged hypoglycemia, increased atherosclerosis risk, and withdrawal syndrome
Timolol
  • No local anesthetic or quinidine-like activity in its individual-drug section
  • Lecture cites a Norwegian multicenter study with a 39% mortality decrease after AMI
  • Also stated to be used to some extent in acute angle-closure glaucoma
Pindolol
  • Nonselective partial agonist prototype
  • Induces less bradycardia
  • Blocks exercise-induced increases in HR and cardiac output
Metoprolol
  • Poor CYP2D6 metabolizers are stated to have at least a 5-fold higher risk of adverse effects than extensive metabolizers
  • Faster recovery from hypoglycemia than propranolol because β2-mediated hepatic glycogenolysis is less inhibited
  • Page 5 says it does not cross the BBB, which conflicts with the page 2 lipophilicity discussion
Labetalol
  • α1 and nonselective β blockade, with β2 partial agonist activity
  • Lecture gives α1:β blocking-affinity ratios of 1:3 and 1:5, and separately notes 1:10 for oral dosing
  • Relaxation of arterial smooth muscle lowers BP without major HR or CO change in the lecture
  • Food increases oral bioavailability
  • The NET-inhibition statement is retained only as a lecture caveat because the trans itself says it does not correlate with Katzung
Carvedilol and Bucindolol
  • Carvedilol: antioxidant effect through attenuation of oxygen free-radical initiated lipid peroxidation
  • Carvedilol: inhibits vascular smooth-muscle mitogenesis independent of sympathetic blockade
  • Bucindolol: peak levels about 2 hours, about 87% protein bound, ↓ PVR and afterload, ↑ HDL without changing triglycerides in the lecture

NICE TO KNOW Other hypertensive-emergency drugs named beside labetalol

Sodium nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blockers, fenoldopam, hydralazine, and esmolol for perioperative or intraoperative hypertension. The lecture also mentions furosemide to prevent volume expansion during powerful vasodilator therapy.

8. Open-Angle Glaucoma
Mark complete
Pages 4, 6–7

MUST KNOW β blockers in glaucoma

Topical β-receptor blockade in ciliary epithelium → ↓ cAMP → ↓ aqueous humor production → ↓ intraocular pressure
  • Noncardioselective ocular agents: Timolol, Levobunolol, Carteolol, Metipranolol.
  • Cardioselective ocular agents: Betaxolol, Levobetaxolol.
  • Lecture preference: ocular β blockers should have no significant MSA or ISA.
  • Use caution even topically in bradycardia, heart block, heart failure, asthma, or obstructive airway disease.
  • Topical prostaglandins are listed as the current drug of choice to initiate treatment, with β blockers commonly used in combination or when prostaglandins are unaffordable.

SHOULD KNOW Other drug groups in the lecture

α agonistsEpinephrine, Dipivefrin, Apraclonidine, Brimonidine↑ drainage or ↓ aqueous secretion depending on agent
β blockersTimolol, Levobunolol, Metipranolol, Carteolol, Betaxolol, Levobetaxolol↓ aqueous humor secretion
ProstaglandinsLatanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost, Tafluprost, Unoprostone↑ outflow
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitorsDorzolamide, Brinzolamide, Acetazolamide, Methazolamide↓ aqueous secretion due to lack of HCO3−

Source-specific ocular note: the lecture says topical β blockers should have no significant MSA or ISA. It links MSA to loss of the protective corneal mechanism and states that ISA can produce continuous contraction that worsens the condition. The lecture does not further explain that ISA statement.
Echothiopate note: the glaucoma table says echothiopate is seldom used because it causes vasodilation and increases intraocular pressure. This is preserved as written in the lecture.

Recall Check

What is the classic nonselective β blocker for open-angle glaucoma?

9. Contraindications and Precautions
Mark complete
Pages 7–8
  • Asthma and obstructive airway disease because of β2 blockade.
  • Acute congestive heart failure.
  • Heart block, including digitalis-related block.
  • Diabetes or hypoglycemia-prone states, especially with nonselective agents.
  • Peripheral vascular or vasospastic disorders.
  • Symptomatic bradycardia and sinus node dysfunction.
  • Abrupt cessation after chronic administration must be avoided.
The lecture concludes that β1-selective blockers are generally preferred when β blockade is required in asthma, COPD, diabetes, or peripheral vascular disease. ISA drugs may be preferred with resting bradycardia. Vasodilating blockers may be preferred in hypertension or heart failure.
10. Adrenergic Agonist and Blocker Response Diagram
Mark complete
Page 7, Figure 2
  • Norepinephrine: ↑ BP with reflex bradycardia.
  • α blocker: reduces α-mediated pressor activity.
  • Epinephrine: biphasic response in the lecture, with an early α component then β effects.
  • α blocker + epinephrine: epinephrine reversal because β2 vasodilation is left unopposed.
  • Isoproterenol: further β-mediated effects.
  • β blocker + isoproterenol: β-mediated response is suppressed.
How to use Figure 2: treat it as a qualitative sequence-recognition diagram rather than an exact calibrated BP trace. The lecture's accompanying bullets emphasize NE with reflex bradycardia, the biphasic epinephrine response, epinephrine reversal after α blockade, stronger β effects with isoproterenol, and suppression of β effects after β blockade.

Commonly Confused Concepts and Exam Traps

Pages 1–8
Exam trap: β1-selective ≠ absolutely β1-specific. Selectivity diminishes as concentration rises.
Exam trap: pheochromocytoma. Do not give a β blocker first. The lecture says establish α blockade first.
Exam trap: glaucoma. MSA is not desirable topically because local anesthesia can remove the protective corneal reflex.
Exam trap: migraine. P-MANT drugs are for prophylaxis, not acute migraine.
Exam trap: sudden discontinuation. Chronic β blockade causes receptor upregulation, so abrupt withdrawal can produce a rebound syndrome.
Do not confuse MSA and ISA.
MSA = membrane stabilizing, Na+ channel blockade, local anesthetic effect.
ISA = intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, partial β agonism.
Do not confuse propranolol, metoprolol, esmolol.
Propranolol = nonselective and lipophilic.
Metoprolol = β1-selective prototype with CYP2D6 variability.
Esmolol = IV, β1-selective, ultra-short acting.
Carvedilol vs labetalol.
Both have mixed α1 + β blockade. The lecture emphasizes carvedilol for CHF and antioxidant / antiproliferative effects, while labetalol is emphasized for hypertensive emergencies and pregnancy-associated chronic hypertension.

Rapid-Fire Final Recall

Whole lecture
1. Core β-blocker mechanism?

Competitive β-receptor blockade → ↓ adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP.

2. First-generation prototype?

Propranolol.

3. β1-selective prototype?

Metoprolol.

4. ISA prototype?

Pindolol.

5. MSA mechanism?

Na+ channel blockade.

6. Shortest-acting β blocker?

Esmolol.

7. Esmolol route?

IV infusion.

8. Esmolol metabolism?

Hydrolysis by red blood cell esterases.

9. Two highly lipophilic blockers?

Propranolol and Penbutolol.

10. Hydrophilic long-acting nonselective blocker?

Nadolol.

11. Major CYP genotype emphasized?

CYP2D6.

12. Why is propranolol oral BA low?

Extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism.

13. β1 blockade effect on HR?

Decreases HR.

14. β1 blockade effect on renin?

Decreases renin release.

15. Why can acute nonselective blockade increase PVR?

β2 vasodilation is blocked, leaving unopposed α1 vasoconstriction.

16. Order of blockade in pheochromocytoma?

α blockade first, then β blockade.

17. Major respiratory adverse effect?

Bronchoconstriction.

18. Most common adverse cardiac effect?

Bradycardia.

19. Why can β blockers worsen hypoglycemia risk?

β2 blockade inhibits hepatic glycogenolysis and can mask adrenergic warning signs.

20. Classic topical β blocker for glaucoma?

Timolol.

21. Ocular β-blocker mechanism?

↓ aqueous humor production through ↓ cAMP.

22. Why avoid MSA in topical ocular agents?

Local anesthesia may eliminate protective corneal reflexes.

23. Performance anxiety drug?

Propranolol.

24. Thyroid storm β blocker?

Propranolol.

25. Does P-MANT treat acute migraine?

No. It is for prophylaxis.

26. β blocker highlighted for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy-related use?

Labetalol.

27. Mixed α1 + β blocker highlighted for CHF?

Carvedilol.

28. Most highly β1-selective agent in the lecture?

Nebivolol.

29. Nebivolol extra receptor action?

Partial β3 agonism with NO synthase activation.

30. What happens if chronic β blockers are stopped abruptly?

Rebound or withdrawal syndrome from β-receptor upregulation and supersensitivity.

31. ISA drugs are less likely to cause what?

Bradycardia and adverse plasma lipid changes.

32. ISA major downside in lecture?

May precipitate angina through tachycardia and increased myocardial workload.

33. Which β blockers are not appreciably metabolized according to page 2?

Nadolol and Carteolol.

34. Which drug has an active metabolite called 4-hydroxypropranolol?

Propranolol.

35. What are the two classic indicators of propranolol β blockade named by the lecture?

Resting bradycardia and a reduced HR rise during exercise.

36. Which mixed blocker has β2 ISA?

Labetalol.

37. Which blocker is specifically noted to have little or no effect on plasma renin activity?

Pindolol.

38. Which newer β blockers are listed as less likely to cause negative metabolic effects?

Carvedilol, Nebivolol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol.

39. Which ocular β1-selective blockers are named?

Betaxolol and Levobetaxolol.

40. What is the lecture's current initial DOC for open-angle glaucoma?

Topical prostaglandins.

Last-Minute 5-Minute Cram Sheet

Whole lecture
Classification
  • 1st gen nonselective: Propranolol, Nadolol, Timolol, Pindolol, Penbutolol
  • 2nd gen β1: Metoprolol, Atenolol, Esmolol, Acebutolol, Bisoprolol
  • 3rd nonselective: Carvedilol, Labetalol, Carteolol, Bucindolol
  • 3rd β1: Nebivolol, Betaxolol, Celiprolol
Key properties
  • ISA = partial agonism, prototype Pindolol
  • MSA = Na+ channel blockade, local anesthetic effect
  • Esmolol = ultra-short IV
  • Nadolol = hydrophilic, long acting, renal elimination
  • Propranolol = lipophilic, first-pass, performance anxiety
Mechanism

β block → ↓ adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP.

β1 block → ↓ HR, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin.

Nonselective β2 block → possible bronchoconstriction and acute ↑ PVR.

Big safety rules
  • Pheochromocytoma: α block first
  • Asthma: avoid if possible
  • Hypoglycemia-prone diabetes: caution
  • Do not stop chronic therapy abruptly
Glaucoma

β blocker → ↓ aqueous production → ↓ IOP.

Classic: Timolol. Avoid meaningful MSA and ISA in topical agents.

High-yield newer / mixed drugs
  • Carvedilol = α1 + nonselective β, CHF, antioxidant and antiproliferative effects
  • Labetalol = α1 + nonselective β, hypertensive emergency, pregnancy HTN
  • Nebivolol = highly β1-selective, β3 agonism, NO vasodilation
Mnemonics
  • NAME CAB = β1-selective
  • APO CAP = ISA
  • PALOCA = MSA list in lecture
  • P-MANT = migraine prophylaxis
